title: FormTranscriptLexicon
description: The form transcript lexicon: the fachlich-observable vocabulary a blind/audio-only user speaks or hears while filling form fields. spellingTokens owns broad accepted spelling aliases; spellingAlphabets and spokenSpellingFormatByLanguage own canonical phonetic output. Number words, diacritic descriptors, connectors, and fillers remain input-side model data. Matching, normalization, rendering composition, and fallback order stay in code; this artifact owns the vocabulary and format facts.

spellingAlphabets.description: Named output alphabets used by phonetic readback. Exactly one German national and one international ICAO/NATO projection are authored; input aliases remain in spellingTokens.

spokenSpellingFormatByLanguage.description: Per-language output formatting for phonetic spelling: named alphabet reference, connector, uppercase marker, and audible names for the supported technical characters.

spellingConnectorsByLanguage.description: Per-language connector tokens between a letter and its clarifier word in spelling mode (iso code -> words: de 'wie', en 'as/for', fr 'comme', es 'como', it 'come'). Language-keyed on purpose: the Romance connectors are short everyday words (a union list would skip 'con'/'come' in every language and shred spelled words that contain them). The per-language values stay aligned with the code-side descriptor's spelling connector per language (model owns the vocabulary; the descriptor picks the output wording).

diacriticsConnectorTokensByLanguage.description: Per-language connector tokens introducing a diacritic descriptor (iso code -> words: de 'mit', en 'with', fr 'avec', es/it 'con'). Language-keyed for the same short-word reason as the spelling connectors.

uppercaseMarkersByLanguage.description: Per-language spoken markers that uppercase the adjacent spelled letter in spelling mode; which side is adjacent is declared by uppercaseMarkerPlacementByLanguage (iso code -> words: de 'gross/grosses' for the German alphabet convention 'grosses M' - STT orthography variants with ss for the sharp s are listed alongside -, en 'capital', fr 'majuscule', es 'mayuscula', it 'maiuscola'). Language-keyed for the same reason as the connectors: the marker words are user-language vocabulary and a union list would let one language's marker mutate values in every other language. A marker with no following letter token is dropped deterministically; case survives composition verbatim and the confirmation readback marks uppercase letters audibly.

uppercaseMarkerPlacementByLanguage.description: Per-language position of the uppercase marker relative to its letter (iso code -> beforeLetter | afterLetter). German and English put the marker first ("grosses M", "capital M"); French, Spanish and Italian put it last ("P majuscule", "P mayuscula", "P maiuscola"). The placement is language vocabulary, not a parser preference: accepting both sides everywhere would turn a stray trailing marker in German - which must be dropped - into an uppercase letter, and requiring the leading side everywhere leaves the romance convention unspellable, so an uppercase-constrained value stays unreachable by voice. A language without an entry is read as beforeLetter.

umlautDescriptors.description: Descriptor tokens denoting an umlaut diacritic (e.g. 'umlaut').

acuteDescriptors.description: Descriptor tokens denoting an acute-accent diacritic (e.g. 'akut').

umlautByBaseToken.description: Base letter/word -> its umlaut form (e.g. 'o' -> 'ö' rendering target).

numberWordsByLanguage.description: Spoken number-word groups per language (iso code -> { units, teens, tens, scales }, each mapping a number word to its integer value). The deterministic word parser is a robustness fallback to Deepgram SmartFormat digitization. de uses within-token composition (dreiundzwanzig); en uses cross-token composition (twenty three). de + en carry the full composition tables; fr/es/it carry the canonical spoken-digit words 0-9 (the units group) as the per-language fallback the digit-capture path consults so an isolated spoken digit digitizes without relying on Deepgram alone.

dateInputVocabularyByLanguage.description: Per-language spoken DATE-input vocabulary (iso code -> vocabulary). de carries the full set: relativeDayOffsets (relative day word -> day offset from today, folded forms incl. the explicit 'uebermorgen' spelling), leadingParticles (optional articles before the day, e.g. 'am/der/den/die'), ordinalEndings (declension endings stripped before stem lookup, longest first), ordinalDayStems (ordinal day STEM -> day number, folded forms with the ss and sharp-s spellings of the dreissig-family listed side by side). Month names are deliberately NOT here: the culture-derived month index stays the single month owner.

relativeDayOffsets.description: Relative day word -> signed day offset from today (e.g. 'gestern' -> -1, 'morgen' -> 1).

leadingParticles.description: Optional leading particles before the day in 'am dritten Mai' / 'der dritte Mai'.

ordinalEndings.description: Ordinal declension endings stripped before stem lookup; longer endings first.

ordinalDayStems.description: Ordinal day stem (ending already removed) -> day of month 1-31 (e.g. 'dritt' -> 3, 'zwanzigst' -> 20).

timeInputKeywordsByLanguage.description: Per-language spoken TIME-input keywords (iso code -> keywords by semantic role). de only: halfHour ('halb' in 'halb drei' = 02:30), quarter ('viertel'), before ('vor'), after ('nach'), clockMarker ('uhr'). Role-keyed on purpose: the parser composes the colloquial conventions from the roles, so the data must keep them distinguishable rather than flattened into one word list.

numberGrammarByLanguage.description: Per-language number-GRAMMAR tokens around the number-word tables (iso code -> grammar): andConnector (the infix the language's composition splits on, de 'und' in 'dreiundzwanzig' - also the fused tens-units infix the spoken year renderer emits, 'neunzehnhundertvierundachtzig'), unsupportedMagnitudeWords (quantity words with no place in the 0-9999 grammar, always rejected as out-of-range, de 'dutzend/dutzende'), signWords (leading spoken minus-sign words; de 'minus/negativ', en 'minus/negative' - only de and en have spoken number input, so only they carry sign words), boundOnePrefix (de only: the bound one-prefix of fused compounds, 'ein' in 'einhundert'/'einundzwanzig', distinct from the free standalone 'eins' of the units table), ohWord (en only: the spoken zero of the century-pair year form, 'oh' in 'nineteen oh five'), hundredWord/thousandWord (the scale words the spoken year renderer composes with, de 'hundert'/'tausend', en 'hundred'/'thousand' - the same words the scales table of numberWordsByLanguage owns for input, kept here as the renderer's composition roles).

dateInputParticlesByLanguage.description: Per-language particles/fillers stripped before spoken DATE parsing (iso code -> words): en 'the/of/on/in' (the English parser calls them fillers); fr/es/it carry the SHARED romance union of leading articles and 'de'/'di'/'du' connectors ('le/la/l/el/lo/los/las/il/i/gli/the/d/de/del/di/du/of') - the romance parser is one union parser for all three languages, so the three entries must stay identical. de is absent on purpose: German strips its leading particles via dateInputVocabularyByLanguage.leadingParticles (one owner per concept).

ordinalDaysByLanguage.description: Per-language spoken ordinal DAY words (iso code -> vocabulary): days (ordinal day word -> day of month 1-31; en 'first'..'nineteenth' plus the round tens 'twentieth'/'thirtieth', fr/es/it the SHARED first-day union 'premier/premiere/primero/primer/primo' -> 1, identical across the three entries because the romance parser is one union parser), compoundOnes (en only: the ones-position ordinals 'first'..'ninth' a tens cardinal compounds with in 'twenty first' - the parser uses this table structurally in its compound branch, so the data keeps it distinguishable from the single-token days). de is absent on purpose: German ordinal days are stem+ending compositions in dateInputVocabularyByLanguage.ordinalDayStems (one owner per concept).

days.description: Ordinal day word -> day of month 1-31 (e.g. 'eighth' -> 8, 'premier' -> 1).

compoundOnes.description: Ones-position ordinal -> ones value 1-9, compounded after a tens cardinal ('twenty first' -> 21). en only.

spokenOrdinalDayByLanguage.description: Per-language SPOKEN (output-side) ordinal day forms (iso code -> day of month -> written ordinal word): de carries the full 1-31 written ordinals the readback voices ('achter Januar' - TTS would read '8.' as the cardinal 'acht'), fr carries day 1 only ('1er'; every other day stays the digit). These are the canonical OUTPUT spellings (unfolded: 'fünfter', 'dreißigster'), deliberately NOT the folded input stems of dateInputVocabularyByLanguage.ordinalDayStems: input accepts folded variants, output emits the canonical form. en/es/it are absent on purpose: they read the digit day.

additionalProperties.description: Day of month (1-31) -> written ordinal day word.

spokenDateConnectorByLanguage.description: Per-language spoken DATE-composition connector (iso code -> word): es 'de' in '8 de enero de 1980'. Only Spanish composes the readback date with an explicit connector; de/en/fr/it juxtapose day, month and year.

spokenTimeFormatByLanguage.description: Per-language spoken TIME-format words by semantic role (iso code -> roles). All five languages carry an entry because every language has a spoken time readback: de clockMarker ('Uhr' in '14 Uhr 30'), en anteMeridiem/postMeridiem (the 'AM'/'PM' suffixes of the idiomatic 12-hour readback), fr hourWordSingular/hourWordPlural ('heure' for hours 0-1, 'heures' above), es articleSingular/articlePlural + minuteConnector ('la 1 y 30' / 'las 14 y 30' - the article carries through to the minute form), it articlePlural + oneOClockForm + minuteConnector ('le 14 e 30' / the idiomatic 'l'una e 30' - the one-o'clock form replaces article+hour wholesale). Role-keyed on purpose: the renderer composes pluralization and the one-o'clock special cases from the roles, so the data must keep them distinguishable rather than flattened into one word list. These are the canonical OUTPUT words; the input-side time keywords live in timeInputKeywordsByLanguage.

choiceConnectivesByLanguage.description: Per-language spoken list connectives (iso code -> connective words) that separate option names in one multi-select utterance (de 'und', en 'and', fr 'et', es 'y', it 'e'). Language-keyed on purpose: the short Romance connectives 'e'/'y' are also plausible label tokens (spelled letters, initials), so they may only split lists in their own language; a union table would shred labels elsewhere.

fillerTokensByLanguage.description: Per-language filler/politeness tokens (iso code -> words) the transcript parsers drop from choice, spelling and digit utterances (de 'bitte/danke/gern/gerne', en 'please/thanks', fr 'merci', es 'gracias', it 'grazie'). Language-keyed on purpose: fillers are user-language words - a blind French user says 'merci', and a German-only union list could never strip it; multi-word phrases (e.g. 'por favor', 's'il vous plait') stay code-side residuals because the mechanism strips single tokens.

commandPolitePaddingTokensByLanguage.description: Per-language polite PADDING tokens of the global and workflow command parsers (iso code -> words: de 'bitte/mal/doch/einmal/kurz', en 'please/kindly/just'). These are imperative softeners around a command utterance, NOT the gratitude fillers of fillerTokensByLanguage - a different vocabulary (the only overlap is 'bitte'/'please'), so folding the two would change matching behavior in both directions. The DATA is language-keyed so per-language consumption stays a possible later modeling decision, but consumption today is one language-agnostic UNION over all entries ('bitte' softens a command even in an English session); per-language application would be a behavior change. fr/es/it carry no entry. Multi-word padding ('por favor') stays out: the mechanism strips single tokens.

digitWords.description: Optional per-language spoken words for the ten digits. Where present, the readback pairs a digit with its word the way it pairs a letter (de '7 wie sieben'), so a digit never stands alone between two spoken segment boundaries. Where absent, the digit is spoken as the bare character. A language that declares this MUST declare all ten, and each word MUST round-trip to its digit through spellingTokens.
